Replacement sensor of the wrong type or fitted in the wrong position
Engine control software with too tight a comparison limit

P2D87.d: Current electric radiator fans carry their own electronics, which turn the PWM or LIN request of the engine controller into motor current. P2D87 means this control module of fan 1 reports that it has become too hot.
s: Fan runs slower or switches off temporarily
Rising coolant temperature in slow traffic
Weaker air conditioning at standstill
c: Worn bearings or debris make the fan motor stiff, so the module overheats from excess current
Clogged radiator or condenser fins, missing air guides, heat build-up at standstill
Ageing power stage or thermal contact inside the fan control module

P2D88.d: P2D88 means the electronics of fan 1 do not behave as expected although supply and communication are present: the module reports an internal fault, or the speed it sends back does not fit the request. Audi documents the code for 2025 Q5, Q5 Sportback, SQ5 and SQ5 Sportback in TSB 2081184/1.
s: Engine warning lamp on
Air conditioning stops cooling
Fan does not run or runs irregularly
c: Poor or wrongly fitted ground connection of the fan
Internal fault of the fan control electronics
Fan blocked or slowed by debris or bearing wear
Moisture or corrosion in the fan connector or LIN line

P2D89.d: P2D89 concerns the power feed of the fan 1 control module: the voltage at its supply terminal, or the value the module reports back, is missing or outside the permitted window. Porsche uses the code in the DME of the 2021–2023 718 Cayman GTS 4.0, Boxster GTS 4.0, Cayman GT4 and Spyder and names it radiator fan 1 (left), power supply.
s: Radiator fan intermittently without function
Reduced air-conditioning performance
Engine control warning in the instrument cluster
c: Engine control software that misjudges the fan supply during start-up (Porsche 198/22)
Blown fuse, loose terminal or high-resistance supply cable to the fan module
Corroded or loose ground of the fan module
Weak battery or charging system dropping the supply during high fan load

P2D8A.d: P2D8A is the second-fan twin of P2D87: the electronics that power fan 2 signal that they have reached their temperature limit. On cars with two radiator fans the second one usually sits on the other side of the shroud; Porsche, for instance, calls its right-hand fan number 2.
s: Second fan slows down or cuts out after long idling
Coolant temperature climbs at standstill
Air conditioning blows warmer
c: Stiff or partly blocked fan 2 motor overloading its electronics
Heat build-up around the module, e.g. clogged fins or damaged air guides
Defective temperature sensing or power stage in the fan 2 module

P2D8B.d: With P2D8B the module that drives fan 2 fails a plausibility or self-test: it has supply and receives a request, yet the status or speed it reports does not fit. Audi's TSB 2081184/1 for the 2025 Q5 family lists P2D8B next to P2D88 and the local LIN bus error U366500, all stored in the thermal management control unit (address 00C5).
s: Engine warning lamp on
Air conditioning without cooling
Fault stored intermittently or permanently
c: Damaged or incorrectly fitted ground point of fan 2
Foreign objects or worn bearings slowing fan 2
Internal electronics fault of the fan 2 module
Water ingress or corrosion at connector or LIN line

P2D8C.d: P2D8C concerns the supply circuit of the fan 2 control module. The engine controller registers that the module does not get proper operating voltage, whether through an open or high-resistance feed, a blown fuse, a poor ground or a reported voltage outside its window.
s: Second radiator fan fails now and then
Air conditioning loses cooling power
Engine control warning displayed
c: Blown fuse or high-resistance supply line to the fan 2 module
Engine control software error at start-up (Porsche 198/22)

P2D8D.d: In a P2 hybrid a disconnect clutch between combustion engine and electric machine lets the car drive on electric power alone and couples the engine in when needed. P2D8D aims at the clutch hardware itself, not at its actuator, pressure sensor or wiring, which have their own codes: the clutch does not take up or release torque the way the control expects.
s: Engine does not couple in or starts with a jerk
Transmission or hybrid warning in the cluster
Limp mode with reduced power or electric-only driving
c: Worn or glazed clutch plates that slip or no longer hold torque
Mechanically binding piston or plates so the clutch does not release fully
Pressure regulating valve of the clutch mechanically faulty
Wrong, aged or contaminated transmission fluid changing friction behaviour

P2D8E.d: Some engines have more than one oil pressure sensor or switch; which one is labelled A, B or C is up to the manufacturer. P2D8E is the general circuit code for sensor or switch C: the controller sees an electrical fault, or with a digital SENT sensor a message or internal error, that it cannot classify as too low or too high.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on make
Oil pressure warning may come on without real pressure loss
Switchable oil pump may stay in its safe high-pressure stage
c: Oil-soaked, corroded or loose connector at sensor C
Internal electronics fault of the sensor or switch
Chafed or broken wire between sensor and engine control unit

P2D8F.d: P2D8F means the signal of oil pressure sensor C lies below its valid electrical range, which usually points to a short to ground, a lost supply or a defective sensor. Audi uses the code on 2025–2026 A5, S5, Q5 and SQ5 models with the 2.0 TFSI EA888 evo5 (TSB 2079097): engine control unit J623 stores it with symptom 17004, and the cluster may show the oil pressure and emission warnings.
s: Oil pressure warning without real pressure loss
Emission control warning lamp
Warning message in the instrument cluster
c: Voltage spike from a workshop charger switched on with the ignition (Audi EA888 evo5)
Signal or supply wire of sensor C shorted to ground
Sensor C defective with output stuck near zero
Engine control calibration that sets the fault too readily

P2D90.d: P2D90 is set when sensor C delivers a voltage above its valid range. Typical reasons are a broken ground or signal wire that lets the input float up, a short to battery voltage or a sensor with a failed output stage.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp, depending on make
Oil pressure gauge or warning shows implausible values
Variable oil pump may stay in its safe stage
c: Open ground or signal wire of sensor C
Signal wire shorted to battery or reference voltage

P2D91.d: P2D91 says sensor C is electrically in range, but its reading does not fit the engine's state: pressure while the engine stands still, too little at speed, or a value that stays frozen while conditions change. Ford's 2024 summary handles sensor A this way under P0521, catching a signal stuck high, low or mid-range and readings that depart from a modelled pressure in either direction for 5 to 10 s.
s: Malfunction indicator lamp after two drives on some makes
Oil pressure warning flickers or appears without reason
Possible engine noise if pressure is really low
c: Sensor C drifted or stuck at one value
Real oil pressure deviation from worn pump, wrong oil or low oil level
Sticking oil pressure control valve of a variable pump
Sludge or debris in the sensor bore

P2D92.d: P2D92 is set when the signal from the phase X current sensor of a belt or crankshaft starter/generator rises above the range the control electronics treat as valid. Such sensors, commonly Hall devices placed around the phase conductor, put out a voltage that tracks the current, so a value stuck near the top of the scale points to the circuit rather than to real current: a signal lead touching a supply voltage, a dama
s: Warning lamp or MIL, often only after the fault has been seen on two trips
Reduced electric assist and weaker restarts after automatic engine stop
Automatic stop-start no longer active
c: Phase X sensor signal wire shorted to a supply or reference voltage
Current sensor output failed at the upper end of its range
Damaged, corroded or water-contaminated connector at the starter/generator
Fault in the evaluation circuit of the starter/generator control module

P2D93.d: P2D93 reports that the current reading for phase Y of the starter/generator has climbed past its upper validity limit. Y is the middle letter of the X/Y/Z set this code series uses; the same list also has U/V/W variants (P2D9B to P2D9D), and no maker explains publicly how it assigns them.
s: Hybrid or charging system warning on the instrument cluster
Boost function during acceleration missing or reduced
Engine restarts by the conventional starter or not at all after auto stop
c: Phase Y sensor signal lead chafed and touching a voltage-carrying wire
Internal fault of the phase Y current sensor in the machine electronics
Defective input stage in the starter/generator control module

P2D94.d: P2D94 completes the high-side series: the phase Z current sensor of the starter/generator outputs a value above its valid window. Inverters for 48 V starter/generators are built for three- or six-phase machines, and the controller relies on measured phase currents to set torque for engine restarts, boost and energy recovery.
s: MIL or system warning lamp
Stop-start and recuperation switched off
Battery warning because the machine charges less or not at all
c: Pinched sensor lead or loose plug at the starter/generator
Water ingress into the machine-mounted electronics
Phase Z current sensor defective, output reads too high

P2D95.d: P2D95 means the phase X current sensor of the starter/generator delivers a signal below the lowest value the controller accepts. The machine works as motor and as generator, so its phase currents change direction and the sensor reports signed values; GM's eAssist table, for example, uses limits of minus and plus 440 A.
s: Warning lamp after repeated detection
Starter/generator runs in a restricted mode with less torque
Stop-start unavailable
c: Phase X sensor signal wire shorted to ground or housing
Sensor supply voltage missing because of an open wire or terminal
Current sensor output failed at the lower end of its range

P2D96.d: P2D96 covers the phase Y current sensor of the starter/generator when its signal drops below the valid range, for instance through a short to ground or a missing sensor supply. For the driver the more important part is how the controller reacts: without a trustworthy phase current it will usually limit or stop electric assist, stop-start can be suspended and charging through the machine may fall back, with a warning
s: Electric assist reduced or switched off
Stop-start suspended
Battery or system warning, charging may be reduced
c: Phase Y sensor signal pulled to ground by damaged insulation
Open circuit in the sensor supply or a backed-out terminal

P2D97.d: P2D97 is the last of the three low codes: the Z-phase current sensor of the starter/generator reports a value under the bottom of its valid window. Because the machine both drives the engine and charges, its phase current is signed, so a low fault stands for an impossible negative reading or a collapsed output, not for a weak current.
s: Warning lamp or MIL, typically after the fault has repeated on a second trip
Electric boost and recuperation reduced or switched off
No automatic engine stop, or restarts via the conventional starter
c: Phase Z sensor signal lead shorted to ground or to the machine housing
Sensor supply interrupted by an open wire or a pushed-back terminal
Phase Z current sensor output stuck at the bottom of its range

P2D98.d: P2D98 points to a phase X current signal of the starter/generator that briefly drops out, jumps or flickers, even though most individual samples may still sit inside the accepted range. That pattern usually comes from a contact that opens under vibration or heat, a chafed lead or an ageing sensor; in many designs the signal is produced by a Hall element sitting in a ferrite ring around the phase conductor.
s: Warning that appears and disappears between trips
Stop-start occasionally unavailable
Electric assist briefly cut during acceleration
c: Connector contact at the starter/generator opening under engine vibration
Phase X sensor lead chafed against the belt drive or a bracket
Ageing current sensor with unstable output at high temperature

P2D99.d: P2D99 is stored when the phase Y current value of the starter/generator behaves in a way a real winding current cannot: sudden steps, dropouts to zero or noise between consecutive samples. The winding inductance smooths the true current, so such jumps implicate the measuring path.
s: Sporadic hybrid or charging system warning
Recuperation occasionally interrupted
c: Corrosion or weak pin tension in the phase Y sensor connector
Harness damaged by heat from the exhaust side or by contact with moving parts
Phase Y current sensor producing a noisy or unstable signal

P2D9A.d: P2D9A marks an unsteady current signal on phase Z of the starter/generator. Before replacing hardware it is worth asking whether the detection itself is too sharp.
s: Battery and engine warning lamps that come on now and then
Mild-hybrid functions occasionally unavailable
c: Starter/generator software with overly sensitive detection, update available
Loose or spread terminal in the phase Z sensor plug
Water in the connector after washing or driving through deep water

P2D9B.d: P2D9B concerns phase U, the first phase of the starter/generator's main U-V-W group, when its current signal is unsteady rather than permanently out of range. GM's eAssist system, whose belt-driven machine appears in its tables as drive motor A, shows how a manufacturer separates hard limits from short events: the U sensor fails high or low beyond 440 A in either direction within 41.6 ms, while a fast, repeated overc
s: Intermittent warning lamp, sometimes only after several trips
Sudden loss of electric assist, returning after a restart
c: Marginal contact in the phase U sensor connector
Phase U sensor lead with damaged insulation or a partly broken strand
Phase U current sensor beginning to fail

P2D9C.d: P2D9C reports an erratic current signal on phase V of the starter/generator. V is the phase that some designs never measure: in a star-connected three-phase winding the three currents add up to zero, so GM's eAssist table runs sensor checks only on U and W.
s: Sporadic system warning on the instrument cluster
Short interruptions of stop-start or boost
c: Phase V sensor plug not fully latched or with fretting corrosion
Intermittent break in the phase V sensor wiring
Phase V current sensor with unstable output

P2D9D.d: P2D9D covers phase W of the starter/generator when its current signal flickers or drops out for moments. The W sensor is one of the two that GM's eAssist belt machine monitors.
s: Warning lamp that shows up mostly when the engine is hot or the weather is wet
Charging through the starter/generator briefly interrupted
c: Cracked solder joint in the sensor path after many heat cycles
Poor contact in the phase W sensor connector

P2D9E.d: P2D9E reports that the voltage of the high-voltage system – the DC network joining traction battery, inverters, DC/DC converter and other HV consumers – has dropped below its lower limit while the system is switched on. P0AFA judges the battery pack itself; P2D9E looks at the network side.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Noticeably reduced drive power or limp mode
Vehicle does not reach ready mode or engine does not start
c: Traction battery deeply discharged or cell groups weak
Main contactor dropping out or precharge circuit faulty
Loose or corroded HV connector or busbar under load
Voltage sensing in the inverter or controller reads too low

P2D9F.d: P2D9F is the over-voltage case: the DC voltage on the high-voltage network rises above the permitted maximum. Too much voltage stresses capacitors, power semiconductors and cells, so controllers react within milliseconds by cutting regeneration or charging.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning and check engine light
Little or no regenerative braking, more wear on the friction brakes
Power limited or HV system shut down
c: Regenerative braking or charging while the battery is already full or cold
Contactor or HV connection opening while the motor generates
Voltage measurement in the inverter or controller reads too high
Voltage limits in control software too tight, update available

P2DA0.d: P2DA0 is the plausibility code of this group: the high-voltage system is neither clearly too low nor too high, but its readings or behaviour do not fit together. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 asks for such rationality checks on inputs, stored separately from circuit and range faults.
s: Hybrid or EV system warning, check engine light
Reduced drive power or no electric drive
Fault appears under heavy load or after a long stop
c: Voltage sensors in battery and inverter disagree
High resistance in an HV connector, busbar or fuse
Main contactor contacts burnt or welded
Calibration or software of a controller, update available

P2DA1.d: With shift-by-wire, the selector the driver touches is an electronic module; module B is a second one, such as a further selector station or a redundant unit. Allison's 6th-generation controls show such a pair: for module 2 they list performance, lost communication, incompatibility and invalid data (P085E, U0291, U0333, U0592), but no supply codes.
s: Shifter warning in the instrument cluster
Range selection at the second selector ignored, vehicle stays in P
Fault appears together with other low-voltage codes
c: Weak 12 V battery or voltage dip during cranking
Corroded ground, loose connector or high-resistance feed to module B
Fuse for module B blown or with poor contact
Voltage evaluation in module software too strict

P2DA2.d: P2DA2 is the over-voltage counterpart of P2DA1: gear shift control module B, the second selector unit of a shift-by-wire system, sees a supply above its permitted maximum. No manufacturer documents P2DA2 publicly or names the limit.
s: Shifter warning in the instrument cluster
Second selector does not respond, main selector may still work
Further overvoltage codes in other modules, flickering lights
c: Alternator regulator or DC/DC converter delivering too much voltage
Jump start with 24 V or charger connected during operation
Module feed shorted to a circuit with higher voltage
Voltage measurement inside module B faulty

P2DA3.d: P2DA3 is a condition code: gear shift control module B reports that its internal temperature exceeds the safe limit. The circuit is fine, the module simply runs too hot.
s: Shifter warning, mainly in hot weather or after long operation
Second selector temporarily ignores range requests
Fault disappears after the module has cooled down
c: Strong sun load or nearby heat source at the mounting location
Output stage for lock solenoid, display or lighting drawing excess current
Internal defect or faulty temperature sensing in module B

P2DA4.d: Coolant heater A here is an electric heater with built-in electronics, usually a high-voltage PTC or wire-element unit that warms coolant for cabin and battery in hybrids and EVs; it is separate from the engine block heater codes P01E8 ff. P2DA4 says that heater's own controller has found a fault in itself – a power switch that shorted, a temperature or current measurement that fails, or a processor error.
s: Little or no cabin heat in electric mode
Engine of a hybrid runs more often just to supply heat
Climate system message, usually without check engine light
c: Power switch inside the heater shorted or failed
Internal temperature or current measurement faulty
Coolant or moisture inside the electronics housing
Software fault in heater or commanding module, update available

P2DA5.d: P2DA5 concerns the feed that powers coolant heater A, the electric coolant heater with its own electronics found in hybrids and EVs. The heater's controller finds its supply input missing or outside the expected window and reports it as a circuit fault, unlike P2DA7, which rates the voltage level of the module.
s: No heat from the electric coolant heater
Cabin heat only when the engine of a hybrid runs
Possibly lost communication with the heater stored at the same time
c: 12 V or HV fuse for the heater open
Corroded or loose pin in the heater supply connector
Poor ground connection of the heater electronics
Supply input inside the heater electronics faulty

P2DA6.d: P2DA6 says coolant heater A, the electric coolant heater of a hybrid or EV, has become too hot. Such heaters measure outlet coolant or housing temperature and switch off above a limit; a Hyundai/Kia patent (US11378000B2) does exactly that, mainly to protect the elements when coolant is missing.
s: Often no noticeable symptom, code found during service
Heater switches off, cabin warms only weakly
Climate system message, no check engine light
c: Software of the controlling module (Ford Lightning SOBDMC), reprogramming
Low coolant level or air trapped in the heater loop
Heater loop coolant pump not running or valve blocking flow
Temperature sensor in heater or loop reading too high

P2DA7.d: P2DA7 is logged when the electronics built into coolant heater A – the HV heater of a hybrid or EV – see a system voltage outside the window in which it may work. While P2DA5 points to the feed circuit, this code judges the level.
s: Electric heater temporarily without function
Fault occurs with very low or very high battery charge
Cabin heat only from the engine of a hybrid
c: Traction battery voltage at the edge of the heater's range (very low or very high charge)
Weak 12 V battery or poor ground of the heater electronics
Voltage measurement inside the heater faulty

P2DA8.d: DC/AC converter control module A is the inverter that turns direct current from the vehicle battery into household AC for sockets in the vehicle; Ford calls it DCACA and uses it for Pro Power Onboard on the F-150, where TSB 21-2127 handles a related fault, P0364 in the PCM. P2DA8 reports an electrical fault – open, short or no valid signal – in the circuit of switch A of this module.
s: AC outlets of group A without power
Message that onboard power is unavailable
Outlet button without reaction
c: Open or shorted wire or corroded connector between switch A and the module
Switch A or its relay failed
Water ingress at an outlet panel in the bed or cargo area
Internal fault of the DC/AC converter module

P2DA9.d: P2DA9 belongs to switch A of the DC/AC converter control module A, the inverter that supplies AC sockets in the vehicle. Unlike P2DA8 the circuit is intact, but the switch does not behave as expected: its signal sits between valid states, or the commanded state does not show up at the output.
s: Outlets of group A work only intermittently
Outlet power switches off unexpectedly under load
Switch position in the display does not match the outlet state
c: Worn, sticking or burnt contacts of switch A or its relay
High contact resistance in connector or outlet wiring
Outlet button jammed by dirt or damage
Voltage sensing in the converter module implausible

P2DAA.d: P2DAA flags an electrical fault in the line of switch B belonging to DC/AC converter control module A, the vehicle's inverter for 120/230 V sockets. The module finds the switch B line open, shorted to ground or to supply, or without a usable signal.
s: AC outlets of group B without power, other outlets work
Message that onboard power is limited or unavailable
c: Open or shorted wire or corroded connector in the switch B circuit
Switch B or its relay failed
Shared feed, ground or converter module faulty (when group A also fails)

P2DAB.d: With P2DAB, switch B of converter module A – the unit feeding the vehicle's AC sockets – fails a plausibility test. Wiring tests pass, yet switch B does not deliver what was asked of it: it stays closed after an off command, opens under load, or reports a position that disagrees with the measured output.
s: Outlets of group B switch off unexpectedly or cannot be switched off
Warning about onboard power in the display
Fault appears mainly with high loads connected
c: Contacts of switch B or its relay welded, sticking or worn
Moisture or dirt at the outlet panel of group B
Load management or software in the converter module, update available

P2DAC.d: P2DAC is the general circuit fault of a second temperature sensor (B) in drive motor A; sensor A has its own series from P0A2A. A motor carries a second probe either as a backup element beside the first – Sensata's hairpin sensor patent allows two NTCs, or an NTC plus a PTC, in one housing – or as a probe on another phase winding.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric drive power limited
Sensor B shows a fixed or missing value in live data while sensor A looks normal
c: Broken or shorted sensor B lead between motor and inverter
Loose, corroded or pushed-out terminal at the motor connector
Sensor B thermistor failed inside the stator
Faulty sensor input in the inverter or motor control unit

P2DAD.d: P2DAD covers a sensor B signal that stays inside the electrical window yet does not fit the situation. CARB asks for rationality checks on hybrid input components where feasible, logged under a code of their own apart from circuit and range faults.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B differs clearly from sensor A after the car has stood overnight
Electric drive power limited in some situations
c: Sensor B thermistor drifted from its resistance curve
Added resistance at a worn or corroded terminal
Probe no longer seated firmly against the winding
Fault in the reference value, e.g. sensor A or coolant temperature

P2DAE.d: P2DAE means the sensor B voltage has fallen below the lowest value a healthy sensor can deliver. Winding probes are mostly NTC thermistors whose resistance collapses as they heat – Thinking Electronic quotes roughly 0.46 kOhm at 180 °C for its stator probes – so with the usual pull-up circuit a near-zero voltage would read as an impossibly hot winding.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows an extremely high fixed temperature in live data
Electric drive power reduced
c: Sensor B signal lead shorted to ground or motor housing
Thermistor shorted internally (often replaceable only with the motor)
Lead pinched or chafed after work on the drive unit

P2DAF.d: P2DAF is the high-side counterpart: the sensor B voltage rises close to the reference. For an NTC probe that would be an impossibly cold winding, so the controller treats it as an interrupted circuit – broken lead, unplugged or corroded connector, cracked thermistor – or, less often, a short to a supply voltage.
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor B shows an implausibly low temperature in live data
Electric drive power limited
c: Open signal or ground lead of sensor B
Connector unplugged or terminal backed out, often after drive unit work
Thermistor open or cracked inside the stator
Signal lead shorted to a supply voltage

P2DB0.d: P2DB0 logs short dropouts or jumps in the sensor B signal that come and go too fast for the steady low and high checks. Because CARB requires circuit monitoring of input components to run continuously, such glitches are caught while driving.
s: Warning light that comes and goes, often after hard driving
Sensor B value spikes briefly in live data
Electric drive power briefly limited on some models
c: Resistance jumps in the sensor crimp at high temperature
Worn or loose terminals in a connector of the sensor B line
Chafed lead with intermittent contact under vibration

P2DB1.d: P2DB1 reports a circuit fault on a third temperature sensor (C) in drive motor A. Three probes in one motor make most sense when each phase winding of the three-phase machine gets its own: Mitsubishi equips the front motor of the 2023 Outlander PHEV with U-, V- and W-phase coil sensors, and a fault on any of them lights both the hybrid warning and the MIL.
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C missing or frozen in live data while the other motor sensors read normally
Electric drive power capped
c: Broken or shorted sensor C lead between motor and inverter
Loose or corroded terminal at the motor connector
Sensor C thermistor failed in its phase winding
Faulty sensor input in the inverter or motor control unit

P2DB2.d: P2DB2 flags a sensor C reading that is electrically valid but disagrees with what the motor should show. With three probes a cold-soak comparison is the natural test: Mitsubishi checks its W-phase sensor (sensor 3, own code P3057) on the 2023 Outlander PHEV once per driving cycle after more than 90 minutes off, inverter switched off, and rejects it when it lies over 26 °C away from the U-phase reading for 0.8 s or lo
s: Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Sensor C stands well apart from the other motor sensors after a cold start
No noticeable driving change in many cases
c: Sensor C thermistor drifted from its resistance curve
Extra resistance at a corroded or worn terminal
Probe loose on its phase winding

P2DB3.d: P2DB3 sets when the sensor C voltage drops below its valid floor. For an NTC probe this would stand for a temperature far beyond any real winding heat, so a short is much more likely than a genuine hot spot: signal lead to ground or motor housing, insulation damaged inside the stator, or a thermistor shorted internally.
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C reads extremely hot while the other sensors look normal
Electric drive power reduced
c: Sensor C signal lead shorted to ground or motor housing
Probe insulation damaged inside the stator

P2DB4.d: P2DB4 is the open-circuit side of sensor C: the voltage climbs toward the reference because hardly any current still flows through the thermistor. A broken wire, a terminal backed out of the motor connector, corrosion or a cracked thermistor are the likely finds; a short to a supply voltage is rarer.
s: Hybrid system warning and check engine light
Sensor C reads far below ambient temperature in live data
Electric drive power limited
c: Open signal or ground lead of sensor C
Terminal backed out or corroded in the motor connector
Signal lead shorted to a supply voltage

P2DB5.d: P2DB5 is set when the sensor C signal drops out or jumps briefly and then recovers – a flickering contact rather than a lasting open or short. No manufacturer documents P2DB5.
s: Warning light that disappears and returns
Brief spikes or gaps in the sensor C value in live data
Fault mainly after long or hard drives
c: Crimp of sensor C changing resistance when hot
Loose or fretted terminals in the sensor C connector
Lead rubbing through and touching intermittently

P2DB6.d: P2DB6 is set when the cooling of a second on-board charger, charger B, cannot hold the unit inside its permitted temperature window, so the charger has to cut its power or stop. No manufacturer documents P2DB6 publicly.
s: Charging power reduced at the charge station
Plug-in charging stops after some minutes
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster
c: Low coolant level or trapped air in the charger cooling circuit
Electric coolant pump of the low-temperature circuit weak or failed
Coolant hoses connected to the wrong circuit after assembly or repair
Low-temperature radiator clogged or its airflow obstructed

P2DB7.d: P2DB7 reports that the high voltage interlock loop of charging system B is broken. Such a loop is a low-current wire run in series through the HV plugs and covers of a charging path; once it opens, the control unit treats the path as unsafe and keeps it switched off.
s: No charging through charging path B
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
c: HV connector in the charging path not fully seated or its catch not closed
Broken interlock wire or pushed-out terminal
Service cover or HV cover of the charger not closed properly
Fault in the interlock evaluation of the control module

P2DB8.d: P2DB8 means the interlock loop of charging system B carries a signal, but one that does not behave as the control unit expects. A common test switches the module's test source on and off and checks that the sensed level follows; a reading that stays put or hovers between the valid bands points to contact resistance, a half-seated plug or corrosion rather than a clean break.
s: Charging via path B refused or interrupted
Charging system warning message
c: Raised contact resistance in an interlock terminal
Plug in the charging path inserted only partway
Corrosion or moisture in an interlock connector
Test source or measuring stage of the module not working correctly

P2DB9.d: P2DB9 is stored when the sensed voltage of the charging system B interlock loop stays too low. Since the module feeds a test voltage into the loop, a low reading usually means current is escaping to ground: a chafed wire touching the body, moisture in a connector, or a failing measuring stage inside the module.
s: Charging through path B not possible
Charging system warning message
c: Interlock wire chafed through and touching ground
Water or dirt in an interlock connector causing leakage to ground
Defective interlock source or measuring stage in the control module

P2DBA.d: P2DBA flags an interlock signal of charging system B that reads too high. A loop fed from a test source and measured at its far end shows a raised level when it is shorted to a supply voltage, or, depending on the circuit, when added resistance or a break lets the measuring input float upward.
s: No charging via path B
Charging system warning message
c: Interlock wire shorted to a supply voltage
Added resistance or partial break in the interlock loop
Faulty measuring input in the control module

P2DBB.d: P2DBB covers an interlock loop of charging system B that keeps dropping out and recovering, so its state flips between valid and invalid. The trigger is usually mechanical: a terminal with low contact pressure, a plug that is not fully latched, or a wire that only loses contact when the body flexes or the parts heat up.
s: Charging via path B stops without warning
Fault comes and goes, often depending on temperature
c: Loose or widened terminal in an interlock connector
Connector in the charging path not fully latched
Chafed interlock wire that loses contact only with movement or heat

P2DBC.d: P2DBC is the general circuit fault of the lock position sensor at charger B's coupler, the feedback telling the vehicle whether the pin that holds the charging plug in the inlet has moved out or back in. B marks a second inlet or charging path.
s: DC fast charging not possible at inlet B
Charger service warning in the instrument cluster
c: Open or shorted wire between lock actuator and control module
Lock pin broken after the plug was pulled while still latched
Corroded or loose connector at the lock actuator
Faulty sensor input in the control module

P2DBD.d: P2DBD is the plausibility fault of the coupler lock feedback on charger B: the signal is electrically valid yet does not fit what the lock is doing, for example a travel that is too short after a lock command, or longer than the pin could ever move with a plug inserted. No manufacturer documents P2DBD publicly.
s: Charging at inlet B refused
Plug cannot be locked or released normally
c: Lock pin broken off or missing, so the measured travel is implausible
Lock mechanism sticking or jammed by dirt or ice
Loose low-voltage contacts at the charger or actuator

P2DBE.d: P2DBE means the coupler lock sensor of charger B delivers a voltage below its valid band. No manufacturer documents P2DBE publicly.
s: Charging at inlet B refused
Charging system warning lamp or message
c: Sensor signal line shorted to ground
Lock position sensor with internal short or wrong resistance
Damaged lock actuator after the plug was pulled while latched
Faulty sensor input in the control module

P2DBF.d: P2DBF is set when the lock position signal of charger B's coupler stays above its permitted range. No manufacturer documents P2DBF publicly.
s: Fast charging at inlet B not possible
Charging system warning message
c: Open ground connection of the lock position sensor
Open signal line between sensor and control module
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty inlet assembly with integrated lock actuator

P2DC0.d: P2DC0 describes lock feedback at the charger B inlet that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing steadily. Because the lock state is a release condition for charging, a flickering signal can end a session or stop it from starting even though the plug is held properly.
s: Charging at inlet B stops or fails to start sporadically
Fault appears only at certain temperatures
c: Loose low-voltage plug at the lock actuator or charger
Sensor wire chafed near the charging inlet
Water ingress into the inlet or actuator connector

P2DC1.d: P2DC1 is the general circuit code for the phase X current sensor of the starter/generator: the controller sees an electrical fault in the sensor path without, or in place of, a separate high or low verdict. CARB's OBD rule normally wants wiring faults and out-of-limit readings stored apart, yet it allows them to share one code when the sensor sits on a circuit board inside the control unit.
s: MIL or system warning lamp
Starter/generator in a reduced mode or switched off
Stop-start and boost unavailable
c: Phase X current sensor on the integrated electronics board defective
Open or shorted lead between an external phase X sensor and the controller
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the starter/generator electronics

P2DC2.d: P2DC2 means the starter/generator's phase X current sensor delivers values that are electrically valid but do not make sense. CARB requires such rationality faults to be detected where feasible and kept in a code of their own, separate from wiring and out-of-limit faults.
s: Warning lamp after the plausibility check has failed on two trips
Less electric torque because current control runs in a substitute mode
c: Zero point of the phase X sensor drifted, for example through ageing or heat
Sensor reference voltage out of tolerance
Phase X current sensor with gain error or slowly failing

P2DC3.d: P2DC3 flags an electrical fault in the circuit of the phase Y current sensor of the starter/generator. Such a sensor needs a supply, a ground and a signal line, and a break or short in any of the three can end up here when the controller cannot or does not tell high from low.
s: MIL or hybrid warning
Automatic stop-start disabled
Battery charged less by the starter/generator
c: Missing supply or ground at the phase Y sensor
Open phase Y signal line between sensor and controller
Phase Y current sensor without output

P2DC4.d: P2DC4 says the phase Y current reading of the starter/generator is inside its electrical limits but fails a plausibility test. One way to test it is an energy balance: the power drawn or delivered on the phase side must match the current on the DC side.
s: Warning lamp after two trips with the fault
Noticeably weaker boost and smoother but slower restarts
c: Phase Y current sensor reading consistently too high or too low
Zero offset of the phase Y sensor drifted
Comparison value wrong because the DC-side current measurement is faulty

P2DC5.d: P2DC5 records a circuit fault of the phase Z current sensor in the starter/generator. A Z phase only exists on machines with more than one phase group.
s: MIL and battery warning
No recuperation and no electric boost
c: Phase Z sensor inside the starter/generator electronics failed
Low-voltage connector of the starter/generator damaged or not latched
Supply or ground fault of the machine electronics

P2DC6.d: P2DC6 is the plausibility code for the starter/generator's phase Z current sensor. The reading stays within its electrical window but does not match what the controller expects from commanded current and machine state.
s: Warning lamp, usually after two trips
Reduced starter/generator output or rough automatic restarts
c: Phase Z sensor has lost sensitivity or drifted
Real current deviation from a poor phase Z connection or winding fault
Controller software or calibration judging the signal wrongly

P2DC7.d: P2DC7 is the general fault for the excitation current of a starter/generator, meaning the DC current in the rotor field winding does not behave as commanded. Only wound-field machines have one.
s: Battery or charging warning lamp
Starter/generator stops charging and assisting
Stop-start disabled
c: Worn brushes or contaminated slip rings on the rotor
Fault in the excitation H-bridge of the starter/generator electronics
Rotor field winding with interrupted turns or a short

P2DC8.d: P2DC8 reports that too little excitation current reaches the rotor field winding of a wound-field starter/generator. With a weak field the claw-pole machine produces little torque and little voltage, so both charging and electric assist fade.
s: Charging warning and falling battery voltage
No electric boost and weak or no belt-driven restarts
c: Brushes worn down so they no longer contact the slip rings reliably
Open circuit in the rotor field coil or its connections
Excitation driver stage in the electronics unable to deliver current

P2DC9.d: P2DC9 means a starter/generator with an electrically excited rotor draws more field current than its controller expects or allows. In such machines, for example Valeo's 48 V claw-pole belt starter generator, the stator windings get their three-phase supply from an inverter, and an extra full bridge sets the rotor's DC field via brushes on slip rings.
s: Check engine light and 48 V or charging system warning
Start-stop and electric boost switched off
Overvoltage protection cuts in, electrical consumers may flicker
c: Excitation driver stage in the controller shorted or no longer regulating
Shorted turns in the rotor field coil lowering its resistance
Faulty field current measurement inside the controller
Field lead chafed and shorted to a supply voltage

P2DCA.d: P2DCA is set when the field current of a starter/generator with electrically excited rotor does not stay steady but drops out or jumps for short moments, without staying beyond the low or high limit long enough for P2DC8 or P2DC9. The rotor coil of a claw-pole machine such as Valeo's 48 V iBSG receives its current through brushes running on slip rings, so worn or sticking brushes and dirty or worn rings are typical s
s: Charge warning that comes and goes
Jerky or delayed restarts after start-stop
Electric boost and recuperation work only at times
c: Worn or sticking brushes, dirty or worn slip rings
Loose connector or terminal on the field leads
Cracked solder joint in the excitation bridge of the controller

P2DCB.d: P2DCB compares the three current sensors of the starter/generator's X-Y-Z phase group with one another or with the DC side. In a star-connected winding the instantaneous phase currents must add up to roughly zero; if they do not, at least one sensor is wrong, even though each may sit inside its own limits.
s: Check engine light with hybrid or 48 V system warning
Reduced electric boost and recuperation in substitute mode
Start-stop may be disabled
c: Gain or zero drift of one phase current sensor
Disturbed supply or reference voltage shared by the sensors
Calibration or software fault in the starter/generator controller

P2DCC.d: P2DCC reports that the rotor position or speed the starter/generator derives from its own sensor disagrees with an independent reference. For a belt-driven machine the natural reference is the crankshaft: engine speed times the pulley ratio has to match machine speed.
s: Start-stop and electric assist disabled
Belt squeal or engine restart via 12 V starter instead
Check engine light
c: Slipping drive belt or weak belt tensioner
Rotor position sensor degraded or shifted
Faulty engine speed reference from the crankshaft sensor or its CAN signal

P2DCD.d: P2DCD is meant for a second particulate filter, labelled B, that the engine control unit finds to be absent or not the specified part, for instance after the filter has been cut out, replaced by an empty housing or swapped for an unsuitable aftermarket unit. No manufacturer documents P2DCD publicly, and makers catch such tampering with other codes.
s: Check engine light on
Failed emissions inspection
Louder exhaust or visible soot at the tailpipe
c: Filter B removed or replaced by an empty housing or pipe
Filter substrate cracked, melted or blown out
Leaking or blocked pressure lines misleading the detection

P2DCE.d: P2DCE reports an open or otherwise faulty control circuit of charging switch B, a vehicle-side switch on the control pilot line. Under SAE J1772 the car first loads the pilot with about 2.74 kΩ, pulling the 12 V supplied by the station down to roughly 9 V; closing a charging switch puts another 1.3 kΩ in parallel, the level falls to about 6 V and the station energises the cable.
s: Station detects the car but charging never starts
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster
c: Broken wire or pushed-back pin in the switch B circuit
Switch or its driver inside the charging module open
Corroded contacts at the charge inlet or module connector

P2DCF.d: P2DCF means charging switch B responds electrically, but the pilot level it creates is not plausible. The only public description of such a test concerns switch A: in a GM check for the Chevrolet Volt, run only while no cable is inserted, the module shuts its internal test switch and the charging switch simultaneously, and the pilot-to-battery voltage ratio then has to lie from 0.14 to 0.28; 30 failures in 50 samples
s: Charging refused or stopping after a short time
Charging error message
c: Resistor in the switch B branch drifted out of tolerance
High contact resistance in switch, inlet or connector
Fault in the pilot voltage measuring path of the charging module

P2DD0.d: P2DD0 says the drive or sense wire of switch B reads below its valid range. The usual reasons are a wire chafed through to body ground or a shorted transistor stage in the charging electronics.
s: Charging starts immediately on plug-in or not at all
Timed charging not followed
Charging fault message
c: Switch B wire chafed and shorted to ground
Output stage in the charging module failed shorted
Moisture in the charge inlet creating a leakage path

P2DD1.d: P2DD1 reports a voltage on the drive or feedback wire of switch B that is higher than it should be. Likely culprits are a wire touching battery voltage or another feed somewhere between inlet and module, or a transistor stage that has lost the ability to pull its output low.
s: Car stays in plugged-in state, station supplies no power
Charging session cannot be ended cleanly
c: Switch B line shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the charging module no longer pulling low
Moisture or pushed-back pins at inlet or module connector

P2DD2.d: P2DD2 is stored when the signal of charging switch B changes state erratically: it drops out or toggles for brief moments, while lasting faults would end up as P2DCE, P2DD0 or P2DD1. Loose terminals, green corrosion at inlet pins or the module plug, and conductors that break contact only when the car moves or temperatures change are the usual suspects.
s: Charging stops and restarts repeatedly
Battery not fully charged after a charging session
c: Loose terminal in the charge inlet or module connector
Corrosion from water ingress at the charge inlet
Chafed wire losing contact with movement or temperature

P2DD3.d: Stuck Off: although the module orders charging switch B to close, nothing changes on the pilot; the voltage sits near 9 V, the plugged-in level, rather than dropping to about 6 V. Through this switch the station thus never sees a request for energy.
s: Car recognised at the station but no charging
Charging error message
c: Switch or relay B no longer closing
Open resistor in the charge-request branch
Pilot voltage measurement in the module faulty

P2DD4.d: P2DD4 describes the reverse case: switch B remains closed against the module's command to open, and the pilot goes on asking for energy at about 6 V although charging should have ended or paused. Welded or sticking contacts, a driver stage shorted on, or software that does not release the switch are all possible.
s: Charging does not end or pause as planned
Charging error message after the session
c: Charger software not releasing the switch

P2DD5.d: P2DD5 reports that the injection path the manufacturer calls B delivers less fuel than the engine control commanded. SAE leaves open what B is: a second injector set, an injector group or a separate operating mode.
s: Check engine light on
Less power, sluggish response under load
Uneven idle
c: Injectors of group B coked or partly blocked
Supply or rail pressure for this path too low (filter, pump)
Airflow or lambda measurement off, so the computed fuel looks too small
Engine control software or injector calibration data

P2DD6.d: With P2DD6 the engine control has found that path B injects more fuel than requested, so the mixture ends up richer than planned. Typical reasons are an injector that drips after closing, a worn nozzle passing extra fuel, or rail pressure above target; a sensor that under-reads airflow can fake the same result.
s: Check engine light on
Black smoke, more frequent particulate filter regeneration
Higher fuel consumption
c: Injector in group B dripping or nozzle worn
Rail pressure above target (regulator, pressure sensor)
Airflow sensor reading low or intake leak after the sensor

P2DD7.d: P2DD7 limits the shortfall of P2DD5 to the cold-start phase. Many engines inject differently just after a cold start, with extra or shifted injections that heat the catalyst or SCR system.
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
Hard cold start, rough running while cold
Longer warm-up
c: Fuel filter restricted, fuel waxing in cold weather
Rail pressure builds too slowly after start
Injectors of group B sluggish or partly blocked
Coolant or fuel temperature signal implausible

P2DD8.d: P2DD8 means path B delivered more fuel than requested while the cold-start routine ran. A cold engine burns surplus fuel poorly, so it leaves as white or blue smoke and raw hydrocarbons before the catalyst is warm, and some of it can reach the oil.
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
White or blue smoke and fuel smell after a cold start
Rising oil level from fuel dilution
c: Injector of group B leaking or sticking slightly open
Coolant temperature signal reads colder than real, too much start fuel
Cold-start calibration in engine control software

P2DD9.d: P2DD9 means the drive circuit of the evaporative leak detection pump is electrically intact, yet the pump does not react the way the command implies: the feedback the engine computer reads back, usually motor current or driver state, does not match the on or off request. Bosch-style DM-TL pumps on European cars are judged by their motor current, first while blowing through a 0.5 mm (0.020 in) reference orifice and th
s: Check engine light on
EVAP readiness monitor stays incomplete
No noticeable change in driving
c: Pump motor worn or sluggish, current draw off target
Corroded connector or chafed wire adding resistance in the pump feed
Water or ice in the pump module (mounted near the wheel arch)
Faulty output stage or current sensing in the engine control module

P2DDA.d: P2DDA is stored when the leak detection pump fails to create the pressure change the leak test expects, as if it never started or moves too little air. GM performs this check on its electric leak check pumps (ELCP) under its own code P145C: at engine-off wake-ups between roughly 4.3 and 11 hours after shutdown the pump runs against a 0.020 in reference orifice, and if vacuum stays under 100 Pa after 60 s on the first
s: Check engine light on
Evaporative leak test never completes, readiness stays open
Possible refuelling message or locked filler flap on some hybrids
c: Pump motor or vane inside the leak check module seized or worn out
Fresh-air filter or vent line of the module blocked by dirt or water
Switching valve in the module not moving, so the pump works against the wrong path
Hose between module and canister split or off

P2DDB.d: P2DDB reports a leak detection pump that keeps running, or keeps moving air, after the engine computer has turned it off. GM names P2DDB in its 2025 summary tables only as a blocking code for the ELCP leak test, while its own stuck-on check runs as P145D: with the pump commanded off, the switching valve is moved from vent to pump position halfway through the test, and a pressure shift above 1,000 Pa within 8 s, or mo
s: Check engine light on
Humming from the tank area after the car is switched off
Leak test results unusable, EVAP readiness incomplete
c: Pump supply permanently live, e.g. stuck relay or shorted output stage
Internal fault of the leak check module (pump or its electronics)
Control wire chafed against a powered line

P2DDC.d: P2DDC is the shortfall code for a third injection path, C. Engines that need it split their injection into more parts than A and B, for example by injector group or by operating mode; the split is defined by the maker, and none documents P2DDC openly.
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power at part load
Hesitation when accelerating
c: Injectors of group C coked or partly blocked
Low-pressure supply weak (lift pump, filter, air in fuel)
High resistance in injector wiring of group C

P2DDD.d: P2DDD flags excess fuel from injection path C: the quantity really burned, as estimated from airflow and lambda, sits above the request. Besides the classic leaking injector, a possible trigger after repairs is a replacement injector whose individual flow code was not programmed into the engine control, so the module calculates with the wrong flow curve.
s: Check engine light on
Dark smoke under load
Higher fuel consumption
c: Injector of group C leaking or nozzle worn
Injector correction code not programmed after replacement
EGR valve not closing fully, too little fresh air

P2DDE.d: P2DDE covers a fourth injection path, D, delivering too little fuel. The letter is assigned by the manufacturer; no one documents this code openly.
s: Check engine light on
Lack of power
Occasional stumbling or misfire-like running
c: Injectors of group D blocked or worn
Fuel supply weak (pump, filter, rail pressure)
Air mass or lambda signal inaccurate

P2DDF.d: P2DDF says injection path D sends more fuel than the engine control asked for. The estimate behind it depends heavily on the air side: if the airflow meter reports too little air, or the NOx or oxygen sensor shows a richer lambda than real, the module sees a surplus that the injectors never delivered, so sensors deserve a check before injectors are replaced.
s: Check engine light on
Black smoke, particulate filter loading faster
Fuel consumption up
c: Airflow, NOx or oxygen sensor reading wrong
Injector of group D leaking or nozzle eroded
Boost or intake leak after the airflow meter

P2DE0.d: P2DE0 is the cold-start shortfall for path C. Its partner P2DE1 is used by Honda, which treats it as a rich fault of its cold-start mixture control: that check compares the ratio the PCM commands just after a cold start with what the wide-band sensor measures.
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
Stalling or stumbling shortly after a cold start
Long cranking when cold
c: Fuel pressure too low at start (pump, regulator, check valve)
Unmetered air entering behind the airflow meter
Injectors of group C dirty, poor spray when cold
Cold-start calibration in engine control software

P2DE1.d: P2DE1 is the only code of this family with public manufacturer use. Honda names it Cold Start Air Fuel Ratio Control System Rich: during the cold-start emission strategy the PCM checks whether the mixture measured by the LAF (wide-band) sensor is richer than commanded.
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
Usually no noticeable driving problem
Oil level above the upper mark possible
c: Injector leaking, extra fuel during cold start
Coolant temperature or airflow signal wrong

P2DE2.d: P2DE2 reports that path D fell short of its fuel request during the cold-start strategy. On petrol direct-injection engines this phase is short and precise: GM's 2025 tables run catalyst heating with a split injection only while the catalyst is under 550 °C, coolant between -12 and 66 °C and the engine has run less than 20 seconds, and they check missing pulses separately under P2B95.
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
Rough idle in the first seconds after a cold start
Often nothing noticeable once warm
c: Deposits on injector tips of group D
High-pressure pump slow to build pressure after start

P2DE3.d: P2DE3 is the excess counterpart of P2DE2: during the cold-start strategy path D injected more than commanded. Nobody publishes this exact code, and the big diesel makers show why it is rare: GM's 2025 diesels judge fuel quantity in the SCR warm-up mode with the ordinary A codes P026C/P026D, keeping only rail pressure (P2C1F, more than 16 MPa below target) and injection timing (P05EC) as separate cold-start codes; For
s: Check engine light on after a cold start
White smoke and fuel smell when cold
Rising oil level over time
c: Pressure regulator sticking, rail pressure too high when cold
Coolant temperature sensor reading too cold

P2DE4.d: Some hybrids and electric drive units can uncouple electric drive motor A from its axle through a clutch, so the motor stops turning when its torque is not needed. P2DE4 means the clutch stays closed although the control module has asked it to open; position feedback or speeds still show a coupled motor.
s: Warning lamp or hybrid/drive system message
Higher energy consumption, electric range reduced
Drive unit noise at speed, possible speed or mode limitation
c: Disconnect clutch actuator does not move to the open position (motor, solenoid or linkage)
Clutch position switch reports engaged although the clutch has opened
Shift sleeve, pawl or teeth jammed or loaded with torque in the engaged state
Control module software or calibration error in the disconnect strategy

P2DE5.d: P2DE5 is the reverse of P2DE4: the module commands the clutch of drive motor A to close, yet the motor stays uncoupled from the wheels. The motor may spin up without the axle following, or the position signal never reaches the engaged state.
s: Warning lamp, hybrid or all-wheel-drive fault message
No electric drive or reduced traction from the affected axle
Combustion engine starts more often, reduced recuperation
c: Actuator motor or solenoid fails to push the clutch into engagement
Clutch teeth blocking on each other, speed synchronisation not reached
Position switch or sensor stuck at disengaged
Worn or broken internal parts of the clutch or fork

P2DE6.d: Whereas P2DE4 and P2DE5 describe the clutch end state, P2DE6 judges the actuator that moves the clutch of drive motor A: its circuit is intact, but it acts too slowly, draws implausible current or does not reach the commanded position within the expected time. No manufacturer documents P2DE6 publicly.
s: Warning lamp or drive system message
Delayed or jerky coupling of the electric axle
Electric drive of that axle temporarily disabled
c: Actuator motor or gearing worn, sluggish movement
Increased friction at fork, sleeve or pawl, e.g. from contaminated fluid
Low supply voltage or resistance in the actuator feed
Position switch or sensor reporting late or erratically

P2DE7.d: California requires a fault found while the cold-start warm-up strategy runs to be stored apart from the same fault found later. P2DE7 is that cold-start counterpart of P26BB for coolant valve C.
s: Check engine light on (after two trips)
Engine and cabin heater warm up more slowly
Usually no change in driveability
c: Rotary valve sluggish from deposits or worn seals
Valve actuator motor or gearing weak
Position sensor reading drifting without a circuit fault
Engine control software needing an update

P2DE8.d: P2DE8 is GM's cold-start variant of P26C0 for valve D, the block rotary valve that sits between two mechanical end stops and meters coolant through the engine block. In the 2025 ECM tables (25OBDG03B) a failure counts when requested and measured position differ by more than 5° while the raw feedback is above 50°, i.e.
s: Check engine light on after two trips
Slow warm-up, weak cabin heating in cold weather
Possibly higher fuel consumption on short trips
c: Block rotary valve sticking in an open position (deposits, wear)
Valve actuator unable to drive the valve to the closed side
Chafed or corroded engine harness to the valve
End-stop learn values implausible after repair or power loss

P2DE9.d: Engines with an electric main water pump run it at a tightly metered speed after a cold start so the block heats quickly. P2DE9 flags that during this phase the pump turns too slowly.
s: Check engine light on after two trips
Uneven warm-up, local hot spots possible
Often no noticeable symptom
c: Worn pump bearing or debris at the impeller slowing the rotor
Low supply voltage at the pump (battery, ground, connector)
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback
Wrong or aged coolant, very thick when cold

P2DEA.d: P2DEA says the intake valves of cylinder 1 do not reach the lift the engine computer asks for, or get there too slowly. It is the first of a row of per-cylinder lift checks.
s: Check engine light on
Rough idle or shaking at low load
Misfire code for cylinder 1 at the same time
c: Switching element or hydraulic link of cylinder 1 sticking (sludge, wear)
Low oil level, wrong oil or restricted oil feed to the lift actuator
Cylinder 1 lift solenoid sluggish though electrically intact
Damaged cam follower, valve spring or lifter on cylinder 1

P2DEB.d: P2DEB singles out cylinder 2: its intake valve lift misses the target or follows a command too late. Lift control for each cylinder separately is the hallmark of electro-hydraulic systems like Fiat's MultiAir, sold by Schaeffler as UniAir: per cylinder, a solenoid decides how much of the cam stroke is passed through an oil-filled chamber to the intake valves; once it opens, the link collapses and a spring takes over.
s: Check engine light on
Misfire felt at idle, cylinder 2 misfire count rising
Reduced power at higher load
c: Cylinder 2 solenoid in the lift actuator responding slowly or leaking internally
Aged, contaminated or wrong-grade engine oil in the hydraulic chamber
Air in the high-pressure chamber after oil starvation or service
Damaged driver stage in the engine control module

P2DEC.d: P2DEC applies only to cylinder 3: the lift its intake valves actually achieve is outside the commanded window or arrives too late. Under the CARB rule, a maker must run a failure analysis of any plausible hydraulic or mechanical defect, naming broken return springs, blocked oil passages and a single cylinder's lift pin as examples, and must catch the resulting errors before tailpipe emissions pass the threshold.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven idle, often with a cylinder 3 misfire entry
Higher fuel consumption
c: Lock pin or switching follower of cylinder 3 not latching
Partly blocked oil passage to the cylinder 3 element
Broken return spring in the lift mechanism

P2DED.d: P2DED is the cylinder 4 member of the per-cylinder lift checks: the engine computer finds this cylinder's lift off target or slow to follow. On four-cylinder engines with hydraulic lift control the oil comes first.
s: Check engine light on
Misfire on cylinder 4, rough idle
Hesitation when accelerating
c: Low, aged, diluted or wrong-viscosity oil
Clogged oil screen in the gallery feeding the lift unit
Oil filter not meeting the maker's specification
Worn cylinder 4 section of the lift actuator

P2DEE.d: P2DEE can only occur on engines with five or more cylinders and means the intake valve lift of cylinder 5 is outside the commanded range or late. Two-step lift reached V6 engines such as the 3.6 L Pentastar, which FCA updated for 2016.
s: Check engine light on
Misfire on cylinder 5
Ticking from the valvetrain on one bank
c: Switching roller finger follower of cylinder 5 stuck in one mode
Oil control valve for the lift switching sticking or contaminated
Oil pressure too low to move the lock pins

P2DEF.d: P2DEF covers cylinder 6, typically on a V6 or straight six: its intake valves do not reach the commanded lift or take too long to switch. Detection follows the same idea as for the other cylinders; for the driver the reaction matters more.
s: Check engine light on
Engine speed limited or lift switching disabled (substitute mode)
Cylinder 6 misfire, rough running
c: Lift mechanism of cylinder 6 stuck in high or low lift
Restricted oil feed to the cylinder 6 element
Actuator for cylinder 6 slow despite correct wiring

P2DF0.d: P2DF0 means that intake valve lift on bank 1 as a whole does not follow the command, rather than one cylinder. Continuously variable systems explain why: BMW's Valvetronic turns an eccentric shaft with an electric motor controlled by the DME, moving an intermediate arm between camshaft and rocker, while Nissan's VVEL uses a DC motor to rotate a control shaft; one shaft sets lift for all cylinders it serves, so a stif
s: Check engine light on
Reduced power, engine may fall back to throttle control
Rough idle across several cylinders
c: Eccentric or control shaft on bank 1 stiff from wear or sludge
Lift adjusting motor of bank 1 worn or weak
Shaft position sensor reading offset or loosened
Air mass meter error or intake leak making the lift appear wrong

P2DF1.d: P2DF1 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2DF0 and therefore only appears on V engines or boxers, on the side without cylinder 1. Nissan's VVEL, used on the VQ37VHR V6 and on V8 engines, is a good example: on the 2014 QX80 V8 both banks carry a separate VVEL ladder assembly with an actuator and a control shaft position sensor.
s: Check engine light on
Uneven running between the banks, possible fuel trim difference
Reduced power
c: Control shaft or ladder assembly on bank 2 binding
Control shaft position sensor on bank 2 moved or faulty
Lift actuator motor of bank 2 weak
Oil sludge in the bank 2 lift mechanism

P2DF2.d: P2DF2 points to the intake valve lift system as a whole rather than to one cylinder or bank, typical for inline engines where one actuator sets lift for every cylinder, as on four-cylinder Valvetronic engines; Toyota's Valvematic also varies lift continuously. Plausibility is usually judged on air flow: a Bosch patent derives the expected flow from lift and engine speed, compares it with the air mass meter and falls
s: Check engine light on
Noticeably reduced power, engine in substitute mode
Rough idle and higher fuel consumption
c: Lift actuator motor or its gear worn
Engine control software needing an update (known on some models)
Eccentric or control shaft stiff from wear or sludge
Faulty air mass reading or intake leak falsifying the plausibility check

P2DF3.d: The clutch between combustion engine and electric machine in a P2 hybrid is only usable when the controller knows where its actuator begins to transmit torque. P2DF3 is a status code: that learned position is missing or invalid, often after a battery disconnect, module replacement, software update or clutch repair, before the learn routine has completed.
s: Warning lamp or hybrid system message
Jerky engine start or clutch engagement
Electric-only driving restricted
c: Learn routine not yet completed after battery disconnect, repair or module replacement
Learn repeatedly aborted because enable conditions were not met
Actuator position sensor delivering implausible values during the learn
Clutch wear or actuator fault pushing the learned value out of its window

P2DF4.d: Electric coolant pumps are usually commanded through a PWM wire or a LIN bus, and pump E is the fifth such pump in a vehicle's lettering; what it cools depends on the manufacturer. P2DF4 reports an open or otherwise faulty command line to pump E.
s: Warning lamp on
Pump runs at fixed speed or not at all
Temperature warning or power reduction of the cooled component
c: Pump connector loose, corroded or with pushed-back pin
Broken command wire in the harness
Pump electronics with failed control input
Faulty output driver in the commanding module

P2DF5.d: P2DF5 means the command line of coolant pump E sits too low, typically shorted to ground, so the module's driver cannot pull it up to the commanded level. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
s: Warning lamp on
Pump stopped or stuck at one speed
Rising temperature of the component served by pump E
c: Command wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the command pin to ground
Internal short in the pump's control input
Output stage of the commanding module defective

P2DF6.d: P2DF6 is set when the command line of coolant pump E stays high although the module wants it low, most often because it touches a battery-voltage wire. No manufacturer documents P2DF6 publicly.
s: Warning lamp on
Pump audible at full speed all the time
Slower warm-up of the affected loop
c: Command wire shorted to a battery-voltage wire
Internal fault in the pump electronics pulling the line high
Corrosion bridging adjacent pins in the connector
Commanding module's output stage stuck high

P2DF7.d: When an electric pump draws air instead of liquid, its impeller loses load and the rotor races above the commanded speed. P2DF7 reports this for coolant pump E; the title already names trapped air as the usual cause.
s: Warning lamp or coolant level message
Gurgling or whining from the pump area
Overheating or derating of the cooled component
c: Air pocket left after coolant service or component replacement
Low coolant level from a leak in the loop
Damaged or loose impeller, rotor spins freely
Implausible speed feedback from the pump electronics

P2DF8.d: P2DF8 means coolant pump E keeps turning, but slower than the module asked for. No manufacturer documents P2DF8 publicly.
s: Warning lamp on
Insufficient cooling or heating of the served circuit
Power reduction possible at high load
c: Bearing wear or debris dragging on the rotor
Air pocket causing the pump to slow or pause for self-protection
Voltage drop in the pump feed or ground

P2DF9.d: P2DF9 covers the hard case: coolant pump E is powered and commanded, but its rotor does not start or comes to a standstill. Brushless pumps sense this internally, for instance from current flowing without commutation feedback, and pass the result to the commanding module.
s: Warning lamp on
No coolant flow in the affected circuit
Overheating warning or power limitation
c: Seized bearing or impeller jammed by debris
Frozen, gelled or sludged coolant (wrong mixture)
Burnt winding or failed pump electronics
Rotor stuck after long standstill, deposits on the bearing

P2DFA.d: Unlike P2DF4 to P2DF6, which concern the command line, P2DFA concerns the power feed of coolant pump E. Smart pumps measure the voltage at their own supply pin and report when it leaves the window they need to run reliably.
s: Warning lamp on
Pump stops intermittently, often with other low-voltage faults
Reduced cooling of the served component
c: Blown fuse or relay with burnt contacts in the pump feed
Loose or corroded ground of the pump
Weak 12 V battery or charging fault
Resistance in feed wire or connector

P2DFB.d: Electric coolant pumps carry their own driver electronics, and P2DFB reports that those of coolant pump E have run too hot. Which loop pump E serves differs between makers.
s: Warning lamp or message about the cooling system
Reduced cabin heating or cooling of the component served by pump E
Pump runs at reduced speed or stops for a while, often together with air or stall codes
c: Coolant level too low or air trapped in the pump, so the electronics lose their cooling
Impeller or bearing running stiff, motor draws high current and heats up
Driver electronics inside pump E faulty or reporting temperature wrongly
Heat shield missing or pump too close to hot exhaust or turbo parts

P2DFC.d: P2DFC states that the liquid loop cooling the high-voltage battery is losing coolant. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
s: Hybrid or EV system service message and MIL
Charging blocked or drive power reduced
Coolant level in the battery reservoir visibly low, possibly traces of coolant under the car
c: Leaking hose, clamp or quick connector in the battery coolant loop
Leak at the battery chiller, heat exchanger or cooling plates inside the pack
Loop not filled or bled correctly after a repair
Level sensor reporting low although the level is correct

P2DFD.d: Some turbocharged and hybrid engines cannot count on intake vacuum to empty the charcoal canister, so an electric purge pump moves the fuel vapour into the intake. P2DFD means this pump does not achieve the expected effect, for instance the pressure or speed it should reach.
s: MIL on, usually without noticeable change in driving
EVAP readiness not complete, emissions inspection may fail
Occasional fuel smell when the canister is not purged
c: Pump connector not fully latched (Nissan Rogue 2022)
Purge pump motor or impeller worn, pump no longer reaches its speed or pressure
Purge hose cracked, disconnected or blocked between canister, pump and intake
Condensation or ice in the intake path, needs ECM update (Hyundai hybrids)
